objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
define and use the terms relative atomic, isotopic, molecular and formula masses,
based on the 12C scale
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: define and use the term mole in terms of the Avogadro constant

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
analyse mass spectra in terms of isotopic abundances
(knowledge of the working of the mass spectrometer is not required)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
calculate the relative atomic mass of an element given the relative abundances of
its isotopes, or its mass spectrum
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: calculate the percentage by mass of an element in a compound

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
define and use the terms empirical and molecular formula

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: calculate empirical and molecular formulae, using combustion data or composition
by mass

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
write and construct balanced equations, including state symbols

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: perform calculations, including use of the mole concept, involving:
- reacting masses (from formulae and equations)
- volumes of gases at r.t.p and s.t.p (e.g. in the burning of hydrocarbons)
- volumes and concentrations of solutions
NOTE:
- Answers to calculations should reflect the number of significant figures given or
asked for in the question. Significant figures should neither be lost unnecessarily nor
used beyond what is justified (see also Practical Assessment, Paper 3, Display of
calculation and reasoning, in Annexe A2)
- Vm = 22.4 dm3 mol −1
at s.t.p
- Vm = 24.0 dm3 mol −1
at r.t.p

(where s.t.p is expressed as 101 kPa, approximately,

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe ionic bonding, as in sodium chloride, magnesium oxide and calcium fluoride,
including the use of „dot-and-cross‟ diagrams

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe the electrostatic forces in ionic compounds as being attraction between
oppositely charged ions

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe, interpret and predict the effect of ionic bonding on physical properties
(including physical state, melting point, boiling point, solubility)
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain the electrical conductivity of ionic compounds when solid, molten or in solution

items.title: (L1)Covalent bonding and co-ordinate (dative covalent) including shapes of simple molecules

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe, including the use of „dot-and-cross‟ diagrams:
- covalent bonding, including molecules such as hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen,
hydrogen chloride, carbon dioxide, methane, ethene
- dative covalent (co-ordinate) bonding, including in the formation of the ammonium
ion and in the Al2Cl6 molecule, CO, NH4
+
, H3O
+

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain the shapes of, and bond angles in, molecules by using the
- qualitative model of electron-pair repulsion (including lone pairs), using as simple
examples: BF3 (trigonal planar), CO2 (linear), CH4 (tetrahedral), NH3 (pyramidal),
H2O (non-linear/v-shaped), SF6 (octahedral), PF5 (trigonal bipyramidal)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
use the electron-pair repulsion theory to predict the shapes of, and bond angles in
other molecules analogous to those specified in bullet 2 above (see section 4.1.2)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe, interpret and predict the effect of covalent bonding on physical properties
(including physical state, melting point, boiling point, solubility)
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain the concept of electronegativity

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain, in terms of electronegativity, the properties of molecules such as bond polarity
the dipole moments of molecules and the behaviour of oxides with water

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the differences between bonding (intramolecular) and intermolecular
forces in covalent molecules

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe that the electrostatic forces in ionic compounds are much stronger than
intermolecular forces in covalent molecules

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe that the bonding (intramolecular ) forces are much stronger than
intermolecular forces in covalent bonding

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe the difference in volatility, solubility, melting/boiling points and electrical
conductivity between ionic and covalent compounds in terms of forces of
attraction (knowledge of hybridisation is not required)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe intermolecular forces in covalent compounds and noble gases: induced
dipole (van der Waals) forces, permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonding

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain differences in physical properties in terms of intermolecular forces,
including:
- noble gases, Br2(l),
- HCl(g), CHCl3(l),
- ammonia and water as simple examples of molecules containing N–H and
O–H groups

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: state that when giant covalent substances melt, covalent bonds break and when
simple molecular substances melt or boil, forces between molecules weaken

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe hydrogen bonds as the strongest intermolecular force yet still weak
compared with covalent bonding

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain the effect of hydrogen bonding on the physical properties of substances,
including ice, water, methane, ammonia, hydrogen fluoride and methanol (for
example, boiling and melting points, viscosity and surface tension)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe metallic bonding in terms of a lattice of positive ions surrounded by
delocalised electrons

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe and explain the electrical conductivity, melting point and malleability/
ductility of metals in terms of their structure and bonding

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe, in simple terms, the lattice structure of a crystalline solid which is:
- ionic, including sodium chloride, magnesium oxide
- simple molecular, including iodine and the fullerene allotropes of carbon
(C60 and nanotubes only)
- giant molecular, including silicon(IV) oxide and the graphite, diamond and
graphene allotropes of carbon
- hydrogen-bonded, including ice
- metallic, including copper

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain the relative energy and temperature required for changes of state in terms
of the relative energy needed to break bonds (with reference to ionic, giant
covalent and metallic substances) and to weaken intermolecular forces (with
reference to simple covalent structures)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe, interpret and predict the effect of different types of structure and bonding
ionic bonding, covalent bonding (giant and simple structures), hydrogen bonding,
other intermolecular interactions, metallic bonding on the physical properties of
substances, including electrical conductivity
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: deduce the type of bonding and structure present from given information

items.title: (L1)The ideal gas and real gases and pV = nRT

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
state the basic assumptions of the kinetic theory as applied to an ideal gas

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain qualitatively in terms of intermolecular forces and molecular size:
- the conditions necessary for a gas to approach ideal behaviour
- the limitations of ideality at very high pressures and very low temperatures

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain that chemical reactions are accompanied by energy changes, principally in
the form of heat energy; the energy changes can be exothermic (ΔH is negative)
or endothermic (ΔH is positive)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain and use the terms:
- enthalpy change of reaction and standard conditions, with particular reference
to: formation, combustion, hydration, solution, neutralisation, atomisation
- bond energy (ΔH positive, i.e. bond breaking)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: calculate enthalpy changes from appropriate experimental results, including the
use of the relationship enthalpy change, ΔH = –mcΔT

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: outline chemical reactions in terms of energy transfers associated with the
breaking and making of chemical bonds

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
calculate energy changes for simple reactions using bond energies

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain why ΔH values from calculated bond energies differ from those obtained
from data booklet and experimentally determined values

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: apply Hess‟ law to construct simple energy cycles, and carry out calculations
involving such cycles and relevant energy terms

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
apply Hess‟ law to determine enthalpy changes that cannot be found by direct
experiment, e.g. an enthalpy change of formation from enthalpy changes of
combustion

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
construct and interpret a reaction pathway diagram, in terms of the enthalpy
change of the reaction and of the activation energy

items.title: (L1)Redox processes: electron transfer and changes in oxidation number (oxidation state)

objectives.objective_text: By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: calculate oxidation numbers of elements in compounds and ions

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe and explain redox processes in terms of electron transfer and changes
in oxidation number

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
use changes in oxidation numbers to help balance chemical equations

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the use of aqueous potassium iodide in testing for oxidising agents and
acidified potassium manganate(VII) in testing for reducing agents from the
resulting colour changes
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to:

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe electrolysis as the conduction of electricity by an ionic compound (an
electrolyte), when molten or dissolved in water, leading to the decomposition of
the electrolyte

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: use the concept of selective discharge to identify the electrode products of
aqueous solutions to include:
- hydrogen ions and metal cations: silver, copper, (hydrogen), iron, zinc,
sodium
- non-metal anions hydroxide and chloride in dilute and concentrated solutions

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe in outline the use of electrolysis in the extraction of metals from acidic
leached solutions, for example copper and manganese
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: construct ionic half-equations for reactions at the cathode and anode

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the transfer of charge during electrolysis to include:
- the movement of electrons in the metallic conductor
- the removal or addition of electrons from the external circuit at the electrodes
- the movement of ions in the electrolyte

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain, in terms of rates of the forward and reverse reactions, what is meant by a
reversible reaction and dynamic equilibrium

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to:  state Le Chatelier‟s principle and apply it to deduce qualitatively (from appropriate
information) the effects of changes in temperature, concentration or pressure on
a system at equilibrium

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
state whether changes in temperature, concentration or pressure or the presence
of a catalyst affect the value of the equilibrium constant for a reaction

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: deduce expressions for equilibrium constants in terms of concentrations, Kc , and
partial pressures, Kp (treatment of the relationship between Kp and Kc is not
required)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: calculate the values of equilibrium constants in terms of concentrations or partial
pressures from appropriate data

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
calculate the quantities present at equilibrium, given appropriate data (such
calculations will not require the solving of quadratic equations)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain the importance of choice of conditions (temperature, pressure, use of a
catalyst) for processes used in the chemical industry including the Haber process
and the Contact process, in terms of equilibrium (yield) and rate

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: interpret data about the conditions used in industrial processes in terms of
equilibrium (yield) and rate

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain, and use, the Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases, including the
use of the acid-I base-I, acid-II base-II concept

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain qualitatively the differences in behaviour between strong and weak acids And bases and the pH values of their aqueous solutions in terms of the extent of
dissociation

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
calculate [H+

(aq)] and pH values for strong acids

items.title: (L1)Rate of reactions and Effect of temperature on reaction rates and the concept of activation energy

objectives.objective_text: By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain and use the term rate of reaction

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain qualitatively, in terms of collisions, the effect of concentration changes on
the rate of a reaction

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain and use the term activation energy, including reference to the Boltzmann
distribution

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain qualitatively, in terms both of the Boltzmann distribution and of collision
frequency, the effect of temperature change on the rate of a reaction
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain and use the term catalysis

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain that catalysts can be homogenous or heterogeneous

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain that, in the presence of a catalyst, a reaction has a different
mechanism, i.e. one of lower activation energy and interpret this catalytic effect in
terms of the Boltzmann distribution
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe enzymes as biological catalysts which may have specificity

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain that reactions which use enzymes only work under specific conditions (pH
and temperature)

items.title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

objectives.objective_text: By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the trends in physical properties down Group 2 including melting points

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe the trends in physical properties down Group 2 including melting points

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the behaviour of the oxides, hydroxides and carbonates with water and dilute
acids
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the thermal decomposition of the nitrates and carbonates

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
interpret, and make predictions from, the trends in physical and chemical properties of
the elements and their compounds
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the variation in the solubilities of the hydroxides and sulfates

items.title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain and use the term ionisation energy
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain the factors influencing the ionisation energies of elements

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe qualitatively and explain the variations in atomic radius, ionic radius and
electronegativity across Period 3 in terms of attraction, number of electrons and
nuclear charge

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe qualitatively and explain the general trend in first ionisation energy across
Period 3 in terms of attraction, nuclear charge and atomic radius (effect of paired
electrons in orbitals of sub-shells is not expected) (see section 1.2.3)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe qualitatively and explain the variations in melting point and electrical
conductivity across Period 3 in terms of the simple molecular, giant molecular or
metallic bonding in the elements

items.title: (L1)Trends in physical properties of elements down a group

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe qualitatively and explain the trends in atomic radius, ionic radius and
electronegativity down Group 2 and Group 17 in terms of attraction, number of
electrons, nuclear charge and degree of shielding

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe qualitatively and explain the general trend in first ionisation energy down
Group 2 and Group 17 in terms of attraction, nuclear charge, atomic radius and
degree of shielding (effect of paired electrons in orbitals of sub-shells is not
expected) (see section 1.2.3)

items.title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to:  describe the reactions of Period 3 elements with oxygen (to give Na2O, MgO, Al2O3,
P4O10, SO2, SO3), chlorine (to give NaCl , MgCl2, Al2Cl6, SiCl4, PCl5) and water (Na
and Mg only)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
state and explain the variation in oxidation number of the oxides (sodium to sulfur
only) and chlorides (sodium to phosphorus only) in terms of their valence shell
electrons
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the reactions of the oxides with water

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe and explain the acid/base behaviour of oxides and hydroxides including,
where relevant, amphoteric behaviour in reaction with acids and bases (sodium
hydroxide only)
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe and explain the reactions of the chlorides with water

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: interpret the variations and trends of the above in terms of bonding and
electronegativity

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: suggest the types of chemical bonding present in chlorides and oxides from
observations of their chemical and physical properties

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: predict the characteristic properties of an element in a given group by using
knowledge of chemical periodicity

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: deduce the nature, possible position in the Periodic Table and identity of unknown
elements from given information about physical and chemical properties

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the addition of water to calcium oxide (lime) to form calcium hydroxide
(slaked lime)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe and explain the use of calcium hydroxide and calcium carbonate
(powdered limestone) in agriculture and manufacture of building materials (cement)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain what is meant by a transition element in terms of d-block elements forming
one or more ions with incomplete d orbitals

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: represent the electronic configuration of transition elements using s, p, d and
electrons in boxes notations (see section 1.2.3)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: recognise that transition elements have variable oxidation states, act as catalysts and
form coloured compounds and that these properties are linked to their incomplete d
orbitals

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: contrast qualitatively the melting points and densities of the transition elements with
those of calcium as a typical s-block element

items.title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
recognise that copper, manganese and uranium are produced from ores in Namibia
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the reduction by carbon of metals from their ores

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the use of carbon as a reducer, including in the production of (impure)
copper from copper oxide and (impure) ferromanganese from a mixture of iron oxide
and manganese oxide in Namibia

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the use of sulfuric acid as a leaching agent for example in the production of
copper, manganese and uranium

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the extraction of pure metals, including electrolysis of leached solutions and
the reduction of uranium ions using magnesium

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: recognize that it is important to monitor and control waste from metal extraction
including:
- sulfur dioxide as a pollutant product from the roasting of metal ores
- waste acids from leaching processes
- toxic metal waste in water and as atmospheric particles

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: discuss the finite nature of metal ores and the benefits and problems of recycling
metals

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the colours of chlorine, bromine and iodine:
- as vapours
- at room temperature and pressure
- in solution

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe the trend in state of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature and
pressure
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: interpret the volatility of the elements in terms of intermolecular forces

items.title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

objectives.objective_text: By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the relative reactivity of the elements as oxidising agents

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe and explain the reactions of the elements with hydrogen

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe and explain the relative thermal stabilities of the hydrides
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to:

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
describe and explain the reactions of halide ions with:
- aqueous silver ions followed by aqueous ammonia
- concentrated sulfuric acid

items.title: (L1)The reactions of chlorine with aqueous sodium hydroxide

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe, in terms of changes of oxidation number, the disproportionation reaction of
chlorine with cold and with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the effects on equilibrium of changes in pH to the reactions of chlorine with
sodium hydroxide

items.title: (L1)Some important uses of halogens and of halogen compounds

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
explain the use of chlorine in water treatment

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
state the industrial importance and environmental significance of the halogens and
their compounds (e.g. for bleaches, PVC, halogenated hydrocarbons as solvents,
refrigerants and in aerosols, see section 4.3.2)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: relate the importance of these reactions to the use of chlorine as a bleach and the
treatment of water in Namibia

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe and explain:
- the basicity of ammonia (see section 2.3.2)
- the structure of the ammonium ion and its formation by an acid-base reaction
- the displacement of ammonia from its salts

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: comment on the depletion of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium from soils by
leaching and farming

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain the lack of reactivity of nitrogen and relate this to the need for the industrial
manufacture of ammonia and its salts for use as fertilisers

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe the changes in the oxidation number of nitrogen in the nitrogen cycle in
terms of the ions and molecules involved, i.e. NH3 (-3), N2 (0), N2O (+1), NO3
-
(+5)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
state the industrial importance of ammonia and ammonium salts for use as fertilisers

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: explain the environmental consequences of using soluble, synthetic nitrate fertilisers,
including their rapid leaching, eutrophication and possible contamination of drinking
water, including from bore holes
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: suggest the benefits of the use of organic fertilisers in terms of their lower solubility

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: recall that sulfur dioxide is an atmospheric pollutant formed from burning fossil fuels
and from the processing of metal sulfide ores
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: recall that sulfur dioxide causes breathing difficulties and forms acid rain

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
recall the importance of the use of low sulfur fuels to keep sulfur dioxide emissions
from vehicles and power stations within the World Health Organisation (WHO) limits
(e.g. the van Eck coal-fired power station at Windhoek)

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: interpret and use the following terminology associated with organic reactions:
- functional group
- homolytic fission and heterolytic fission
- free radical, initiation, propagation, termination
- nucleophile, electrophile
- addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation
- oxidation and reduction

By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: 
recall and use systematic nomenclature to name alkanes, alkenes,
halogenoalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and
amines, with chain length up to six carbon atoms, including:
- numbering the carbon atoms in a direction to give the lowest prefix possible e.g.
1-chlorobutane (not 4-chlorobutane)
- the use of the prefixes mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa-.
(in equations for organic redox reactions, the symbols [O] and [H] are acceptable for
oxidising and reducing agents)

items.title: (L1)Shapes of organic molecules AND Infra-red spectroscopy

objectives.objective_text:
By the end of this lesson the Chemistry Advanced Subsidiary level Learner should be able to: describe and explain the shape of, and bond angles in, the ethane and ethene
molecules in terms of electron pair repulsion theory (including relative length of
bonds between carbon atoms) (see section 1.3.2)
